name: Moshood Abiola Balogun
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Nigerian national. The applicant alleged that deportation to Nigeria would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the treaty. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was decided on 9 March 2010 and the decision was published on 10 March 2010. The decision was made to allow the applicant to remain in the UK pending the Court’s decision. It was also decided that the case should be heard on the merits and admissible.

Indefinite leave to remain was granted to the applicant, outside the immigration rules, on 1 December 2003. He was convicted on 21 February 2007 of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced into letting his premises be used for the preparation and sale of drugs by a group of people whom he feared. The applicant was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, and on 18 October 2007 was notified of the Secretary of State’s intention to deport him.

The applicant appealed against the decision to deport him and his appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on 13 March 2008. Law Lords rejected the applicants’ argument that, given the criminal law context, a strict approach to the construction of section 72A of the CJA 1988 should be adopted. They noted that section 71(1) of the CDA 1988 imposed a positive duty to proceed with confiscation proceedings. They also noted that the time limits under sections 72A were linked to the date of conviction rather than sentence. This was considered to be evidence that Parliament's intention was the early disgorgement of an offender's criminal gains. Though no common law power to adjourn existed, Parliament could not have intended to disable a court from making a confiscation order after sentence merely because the time-limits were not strictly adhered.

Two British nationals, Mr David Frederick Bullen and Mr Kamlesh Kumar Soneji (‘the applicants’), were charged with involvement in a money laundering scheme. On 14 June 2007 the Acting President of the Chamber of the Fourth Section to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time (Article 29 §3) The applicants were represented by Mr N. Seeley, a lawyer practising in Hertford. The confiscation hearing was fixed for 30 October 2000, outside the six-month period required under section 72A of the CJA 1988. The applicants objected that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the confiscation proceedings on the grounds that more than six months had elapsed since their convictions. It was agreed by the parties that the proceedings should be adjourned to await the outcome of a similar case which was due to be heard by the Court of Appeal, R v Steele and Shevki. On 24 November 2000 both the applicants’ applications for leave to appeal against sentence were refused by a single judge of the court. On 31 January 2001 the confiscative proceedings were listed again for mention. Renewal of argument in relation to the Crown Court’s jurisdiction was listed for 8 and 9 March 2001. The Court of Appeal heard and dismissed Mr E’s appeal against conviction. Mr E. was seeking leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The substantive hearing of the confiscation hearing was again adjourned. Crown Court imposed a confiscation order on the second applicant in the amount of GBP 75,350, with a consecutive term of twelve months’ imprisonment to be served in default. The first applicant lodged an application for leave. to appeal challenging the confiscate order on same grounds as the second. applicant (see paragraph 20 above). The proceedings were adjourned to 28 January 2002 with a time estimate of three weeks. The Court of Appeal quashed the confiscation orders and default sentences of imprisonment. The court ruled that a high degree of judicial scrutiny was required before finding exceptional circumstances to justify the imposition of a confiscation order outside the six-month time-limit. They noted that on 29 June 2000, defence counsel for the second applicant and the co-accused Mr. E. had requested an early hearing at the Crown Court. The earliest date that the trial judge would be available was the week beginning 30 October 2000. That date was pencilled in, even though it was “more than four months away”. Neither had there been any analysis of any factors which might amount to exceptional circumstances. The trial judge had also “candidly acknowledged more than once” that there were no exceptional circumstances in the present case. The Court of Appeal certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decisions. The House of Lords observed that the core problem before it was whether, as a matter of statutory construction, failure to comply with a statutory time-limit would have the effect of invalidating an act. In London and Clydeside Estates Ltd v. Aberdeen District Council [1980] 1 WLR 182, 189E-190C, Lord Hailsham had emphasised that it was within the courts’ inherently discretionary jurisdiction to determine the nature of a particular statutory requirement and to examine the consequences of non-compliance before determining whether Parliament had intended total invalidity. The Court of Appeal re-imposed the confiscation orders and sentences of imprisonment in default on the applicants in October 2005. The prejudice to the applicants was not significant and was outweighed by the countervailing public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for what were no more than bona fide errors in the judicial process. In any event, there would always be the safeguard of judicial review should there be an apparent abuse of process. The court ruled that a strict approach to the construction of section 72A of the CJA 1988 should be adopted and instead applied a teleological approach. The case was heard at the High Court in London.

Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The case was brought against the insurance company by a Polish man. The case was adjourned until at least 4 December 2000. The Warsaw Regional Court gave judgment on 15 January 2001 and ordered the company to pay PLN 25,000 to the applicant. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Warsaw Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny), claiming a higher amount of compensation. The court dismissed the appeal on 25 April 2005 as manifestly ill-founded. The current proceedings are pending before the Regional Court. The application was dismissed on 3 March 2005 under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about the right to a trial within a reasonable time.

The first applicant was found guilty on two of the charges and was sentenced to 4 years' imprisonment and to be dismissed with disgrace. The second applicant was convicted on three charges and sentenced to 5 years' prison. Both applicants applied to the single judge of the Courts-Martial Appeal Court (“CMAC”) for leave to appeal to that court against conviction and sentence. The applicants petitioned the Defence Council against conviction. By letters dated 18 February 1998 and 27 February 1997, their representatives were informed of the decisions (taken by the Army Board) to reject their petitions.

A soldier of the regular forces of the British Army was charged with wounding with intent and inflicting grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment and to be discharged from the army. He appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court. A single judge granted leave to appeal to the full CMAC. A second judge rejected his appeal. The third applicant appealed again to the courts-martial appeal court. All three appeals were rejected by the courts. A third application was made to the Supreme Court of the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant was acquitted of the first charge and convicted of the second. The appeal was dismissed.

The applicant was a soldier of the regular forces of the British Army. He was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment and to be discharged from the army. He argued that he had not had a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The single judge granted leave to appeal to the full CMAC. The Courts-Martial Appeal Court (all three applicants) ruled in favour of the applicant and the other two. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the grounds of appeal were not arguable. The case has been referred to as the ‘Findlay case’ by the Appeal Court.

A soldier of the regular forces of the British Army was charged with wounding with intent and inflicting grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment and to be discharged from the army. The single judge granted leave to appeal to the full CMAC. a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal (referring also to the Findlay judgment). The Courts-Martial Appeal Court (all three applicants) ruled that the grounds of appeal were not arguable. The appeal was settled by a three-judge panel which ruled in favour of all three applicants. The court-martial was held in London, and the case was heard in London and Manchester.

Ministry of Defence explained that neither the presidents nor the members of the applicants' courts-martial had been under the command of the convening officer. A policy decision had been taken that, as from 1 January 1996, all courts-Martial would be composed of a president and members who were not in the chain of command. The applicants' appeals were rejected by detailed judgment of 13 November 1998. The CMAC considered that there was no possible reason to intervene. It noted that the time for having regard to the provisions of the Convention had not yet been reached, but it was difficult to see, even in such circumstances, how the provision of Article 6 could be of any assistance to the applicants.

Ministry of Defence explained that neither the presidents nor the members of the applicants' courts-martial had been under the command of the convening officer and that none had been subordinate to him in the chain of command. Convening officer would not have reported on either the president or the members in their annual confidential reports. CMAC noted the change in policy as regards the constitution of courts-Martial in place since January 1996. They considered that there was no chain ofcommand influence and no obvious reason why any observer would suspect any lack of independence or impartiality. They said the reliance on the Findlay judgment was misconceived as the only power of the CMAC was to enquire whether the convictions were unsafe.

The applicants were represented by Mr G. Blades, a lawyer practising in Lincoln. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agents, Mr C. Whomersley and, subsequently, Mr J. Grainger. On 26 September 2000 the Court decided to join and communicate the applications to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. The applicants petitioned the Defence Council against conviction and sentence. The first applicant pointed to various alleged failings by the judge advocate during the court-martial and argued that his sentence was excessive. The second applicant argued before the single judge that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal (referring also to the Findlay judgment). The single judge granted leave to appeal to the full CMAC. The third applicant was charged (pursuant to section 70 of the Army Act 1955) with wounding with intent contrary to section 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. He was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment and to be discharged from the British Army. He was informed that the Reviewing Authority had decided not to waive the relevant time-limit which had by then expired. His application to the single judge of the CMAC was dated 18 July 1997 and raised the Findlay issue together with the fact that he could not appeal against sentence only to CMAC. On 6 October 1997 the singleJudge rejected that application considering that the grounds of appeal were not arguable. He renewed his application for leave to appeal to the full CMAC raising the same points. The applicants' appeals were rejected by detailed judgment of 13 November 1998. The Courts-Martial Appeal Court (all three applicants) unanimously rejected their appeals. The time for having regard to the provisions of the Convention had not yet been reached. It was difficult to see, even in such circumstances, how the provisions could be of any assistance to the applicants. It noted that the time was not yet right to make such a decision. The decision was made to extend the deadline to December 31, 2014. The deadline was extended again to December 28, 2014, if no action was taken by the parties to the case before the end of the current session of the European Court of Human Rights. The ruling was made in favor of a temporary extension of the deadline until December 29, 2013, and until December 30, 2013. The applicant, Mr Abdurrahman Şiray, is a Turkish national who was born in 1972 and lives in Siirt. On 20 June 2003 the applicant, who is of Kurdish origin, was arrested in Mardin and taken into police custody with three other individuals on suspicion of acting as a courier for an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK/KADEK. In his statement, given in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant denied any affiliation with the illegal organisation and contested F.A’s allegations. The applicant was brought before the Nusaybin Public Prosecutor on 23 June 2003. He denied the charges against him, but confirmed that the statements he had made during his detention in police custody were accurate. On 7 July 2003 the Public Prosecutor filed an indictment with that court accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK, and F.A. of membership of that organisation. On 19 August 2003 the Diyarbakır State Security Court held its first hearing, at which the applicant informed the court that he did not have sufficient knowledge of Turkish to follow the hearings. The court bailiff, who spoke Kurdish, was therefore appointed as interpreter. At the sixth hearing, held on 1 April 2004, the applicant’s lawyer requested his release. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court. The applicant was found guilty as charged and convicted under Article 169 of the former Criminal Code and Section 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act for aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK. He was sentenced to four years and six months' imprisonment. On 22 December 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The case was examined again in view of the recent legislative changes to the Criminal Code. The new Criminal Code which had entered into force on 1 June 2005 (Law no. 5237) had provisions more favourable to the applicant.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the German Government on 10 August 1992 and by the European Commission of Human Rights on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15473/89) against Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 on 11 July 1989. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3 and 8 (art. 3, art. 8) of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The President gave the lawyer leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 March 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig for the Government, by Mr Frowein for the Commission and by Mr Stüben for the applicants, as well as replies to its questions and by two of its members individually. The applicants' lawyer, the Agent of the Government and the Delegate of the Commission were all present. The applicant was accused of driving through a red traffic light and of trying to get away - an allegation denied by the applicant. The Commission's observations were produced by the Commission on 4 February 1993 and by the Government on 24 February 1993. Mrs Klaas agreed to have a blood sample taken, but explained that she wished first to accompany her daughter to a neighbour. One of the police officers refused to allow this and dragged her to the police car. She was then driven to the hospital for the blood test, which showed the level of alcohol in her blood to be 0.82 per ml. The precise course of the events is disputed by the applicants (see paragraph 7 below) and the policeOfficers (see paragraphs 9 and 10 below) The first applicant underwent two medical examinations. On 11 February 1986, Dr Schwering certified that he had examined the applicant on 29 January and noticed bruises which were about 10cm long on her right arm. He also stated that she would suffer long-term problems, in particular with her left shoulder. Police Constable Bolte stated in his report that after Mrs Klaas had been informed that she had to undergo a blood test, she had attempted to escape into the darkness of the back-yard. The applicant had been very aggressive. When told that she was to be arrested she had suddenly calmed down and declared that she would come along when she had taken her daughter, whom he had assumed to be about twelve years old, to a neighbour. The police officers had agreed in order to avoid a further escalation of the events. The criminal proceedings against the first applicant were discontinued by the public prosecutor’s office (Staatsanwaltschaft) at the Detmold Regional Court. On 24 April 1986 the first applicant laid an information against the police officers concerned. She alleged that they had assaulted her contrary to Articles 223 and 230 of the Criminal Code. A driving ban of one month was also imposed. On 18 September 1986, the Head of the Detmold District Administration, acting as the Police Department authority (Kreispolizeibehörde), dismissed her complaint. The first applicant’s subsequent appeal to the Hamm Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) and to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), were also dismissed. The case is still ongoing. The first applicant instituted civil proceedings in April 1987 against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia and the police officers concerned. She claimed compensation for the injuries sustained on 28 January 1986. Her request to take her daughter to a neighbour’s first was granted. When the first applicant opened the door and tried to enter with her daughter, one of the police. officers held her right arm fast, whereupon she started to kick and to hit out with her left hand. She had to be handcuffed. It was not accepted that her head knocked against the window-ledge at any moment in the course of the arrest. The judge concluded that the use of force had been justified and was not disproportionate to the aim pursued. Police Constable Wildschut confirmed the general circumstances of the first applicant’s arrest as described by Police Constable Bolte. He could not remember who had kept hold of Mrs Klaas until they had put her into the police car, or whether she had bent forward suddenly owing, for instance, to a jerking on her handcuffs and the resulting pain. He confirmed that she had requested that the handcuffs be removed but did not remember her complaining about any pain - in particular pain in her left shoulder. Finally, the second applicant, Monika, gave evidence. She stated that she remembered the incident and that she was not injured in any way. Monika was arrested with her mother and the police officers in their back-yard. Her mother had rung the doorbell and opened the door using a key. Monika had then gone into the house and closed the door behind her. She said that she had managed to see through the plain glass door panel that one of the police officer had pushed her mother’s head against the wall. The officer concerned had blond hair. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion. The Detmold Regional Court dismissed the first applicant's compensation claims against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia. The plaintiff was under suspicion of driving under the influence of alcohol in road traffic contrary to Article 316 of the Criminal Code. The arrest itself was not unlawful. The Chamber is not convinced that the police officers caused the plaintiff’s injuries by exceeding what was necessary when arresting her. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff's daughter, conflicts. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police. officers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her. Witness Klaas claims to have seen one of the police officers repeatedly knocking the plaintiff’s head against the wall by the door, the two police officers deny this. None of these three witnesses can be regarded as not having an interest in these proceedings. Neither the balance of probability nor general experience militate in favour of accepting the plaintiff's version of events. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the walls; the shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled while being restrained by the police and when the handcuffs were being put on her. For these reasons the claim must be dismissed. Monika Klaas, the second applicant, contended that the aforementioned treatment of her mother in her presence had violated her right to respect for her private and family life. James and Sarah Boyle are British citizens born in 1944 and 1950 respectively. In 1967, the first applicant was sentenced in Scotland to life imprisonment for murder. In March 1973, Mr. Boyle was removed from Peterhead Prison to a Special Unit in Barlinnie Prison. This Unit had been set up on an experimental basis to treat selected long-term prisoners and prisoners with violent propensities (see paragraph 32 below). It was considered that, although the regime there was on traditional traditional terms and conditions, Mr Boyle had special abilities. In the opinion of the Supreme Court, the application of section 42 par. 1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason. Section 42 is not at all meant to be used to terminate proceedings when it is certain that an offence cannot be proved on the facts or does not exist in law. The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. In point of fact, by reason of its basic legal character, any decision can only be understood in one way: further clarification of, and possible prosecution in, a case which is already recognisable as being a trifling matter is to be avoided.

In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. If sufficient grounds for prosecuting the individual in question are lacking, the public prosecutor shall take no further action on the complaint and shall transmit the file to the investigating judge, together with a statement to the effect that he sees no reason to continue with the prosecution. The judge must then terminate the preliminary enquiries (section 90 par. 1). This provision applies, mutatis mutandis, to district court. proceedings.

He contested the doctor's findings, claiming in particular that the latter had based his opinion on information that was contradicted by the material in the case-file (aktenwidrig) Mr. Adolf called on the District Court either to acquit him after trial or to terminate the proceedings pursuant to section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 21 below). He requested that fresh medical evidence be taken forthwith. The District Court notified an associate of the applicant's lawyer that the proceedings had been terminated - on an unspecified date - in pursuance of section 451 2 of the Criminal Procedure. Irma Proxauf alleged that the accused had caused her an injury, namely a bruise on her left arm and another below her left breast, with a bunch of keys. The key first struck the back of the right hand, causing a superficial abrasion, and then bounced against the left side of the above-named person's chest. No injury could be established on the chest. The injury found (festgestellte) is insignificant as it does not exceed the three-day limit. The fault (Verschulden) of the accused may be described as insignificant (geringfügig) and his character gives cause to expect that he will conduct himself properly in future. The conditions of section 42 of the Penal Code are met, justifying the above decision. The Generalprokurator said that section 42 of the Penal Code was not appropriate where, on the basis of the complaint or the preliminary enquiries, no offence could be established on the facts or existed in law. In both cases, he said, the decisions would be taken without the formal hearing of evidence (Beweisverfahren), something which, as followed in any event from Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention, should in principle precede any finding of guilt (Schulderkenntnis) A court decision terminating proceedings in accordance with section 42 could therefore only be grounded on a “suspected state of affairs’ (Verdachtslage) as disclosed by the case-file. Mr. Adolf moved the Supreme Court to hold that the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated 10 January 1978 was contrary to the law. He relied on section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which places the judge under a duty to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 of the Penal Code are met. Mr. Adolf criticised the District Court for having failed to take into consideration evidence in his favour, for having declined to hear witnesses requested by him and for not having given him the opportunity to challenge the expert medical opinion. He alleged a breach of Article 6 par. 1 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, 6-3-d) of the Convention. The Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on 28 February 1980. In the opinion of the Supreme Court, the application of section 42 par. 1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason. Section 42 is not at all meant to be used to terminate proceedings when it is certain that an offence cannot be proved on the facts or does not exist in law. The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. Since legal proof of the suspect's guilt is not the object pursued under section 42, the decision is to be avoided in the interests of procedural economy. The judgment of the Supreme Court was reproduced in an Austrian legal journal but the applicant's identity was not revealed. The professional association to which Mr. Adolf belongs has not instituted any disciplinary proceedings against him in respect of the facts underlying Mrs. Proxauf's complaint. The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of a medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The public prosecutor (Staatsanwalt) is required by law to inquire into the correctness of any report (Anzeige) of an offence for which a prosecution must be brought. In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. In cases before a district court, the decision terminating proceedings is governed by section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides: “If the court is satisfied that the conditions laid down in section 42 are met, it shall terminate the proceedings by a decision.’’ The decision whether or not the conditions of paragraph (1) hereof are met shall be taken by the court; where the court decides in the affirmative, it Shall bring the proceedings to a close.  section 42 is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases, notably for reasons of procedural economy. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. As a result of the present case, two circulars were issued on 15 January 1979 and 24 March 1980 by the relevant Austrian authorities drawing the attention of the courts to the problems raised. The Commission accepted the application on 6 July 1979. In its report of 8 October 1980 (Article 31 of the Convention) (art. 31), the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been breach of paragraph 2 of Article 6. The report contains three dissenting opinions. At the close of the hearings held on 24 November 1981, the Agent of the Government made “a final submission and a formal motion, namely that the Court, when considering this matter, come to the conclusion that, in the present case, there was no violation of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms in all three aspects which have been mentioned“.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the execution of the preventive detention order against him had violated Articles 5 and 14. The Government of Bulgaria, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant entered Germany in 1979. He has been convicted some fifteen times since 1980, notably of theft and burglary. He is currently detained in Grad Vraca (Bulgaria) The applicant was arrested and remanded in detention in December 1994. He was convicted of eight counts of burglary and attempted burglary. The city of Munich ordered the applicant’s expulsion to Bulgaria and prohibited him to re-enter Germany for an indefinite duration in view of his criminal convictions. He served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he has been held in preventive detention. The applicant is now eligible for release after serving his prison sentence. He is also eligible for parole from prison once he has served his sentence. The application for parole was denied by the Erlangen Prison authorities on 7 January 2002 because he was liable to be expelled after being released from prison. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. The refusal of the Straubing Prison authorities to allow the applicant’s defence counsel to inspect his personal files had violated the right to a fair trial. On 26 February 2004 the Regensburg Regional Court, having heard the applicant on 15 January 2004 and the applicant and the two experts W. and T. on 19 February 2004, decided that the execution of the applicant's preventive detention was necessary in view of its objective. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The Public Prosecutor’s Office would have to consider this issue when deciding on a fresh motion lodged by the applicant to suspend his preventive detention pursuant to Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 45 below). Otherwise, a suspension of the preventive detention order against the applicant on probation could have to be ordered in the future for reasons of proportionality even without the conditions of his detention having previously been relaxed. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint and to grant him legal aid. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that due to the applicant's persistent refusal to accept responsibility for his offences there were no suitable measures to prepare him adequately for his release. The judge found that this was not the case in this case. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. It conceded that it was problematic that no measures at all were planned by the prison authorities to further the applicant's reintegration into society. The applicant could not expect any relaxations in the conditions of his detention. In practice, the latter were a precondition for coming to an assessment that a detainee was no longer dangerous to the public. Therefore, the court would have to decide at the next periodic review of his preventive detention whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations. Munich Court of Appeal found that the balancing between the public interest in the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention and his interest in his personal liberty had – at least at that time – not been unconstitutional. The applicant, who was born in 1926, was convicted of manslaughter by the Central Criminal Court, London in 1987. The naked body of the victim, a neighbour of the applicant, was discovered outside the door of her flat wrapped in a bedspread. The applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. He was released in August 1988. On 2 January 1996 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of attempted rape of his next-door neighbour. He maintained that he had had sexual intercourse with the woman with her consent and the woman claimed that the incident had taken place after she had blacked out from drinking. On 11 July 1997 the Court of Appeal rejected his appeal against sentence. The trial court deducted the period of his pre-trial detention from the sentence imposed pursuant to the Criminal Justice Act 1967.

The applicant was born in 1958 and lives in Charlottenlund. At the relevant time the applicant was part owner of a private limited stockbrokers company. On 18 January 1994 he learnt that the tax authorities were about to check the company’s accounts for the years 1989 to 1992. On 17 June 1996, the Copenhagen City Court (Københavns Byret – hereafter ‘the City Court’), sitting in camera, granted the police a warrant to search the premises of the applicant's business. On 2 July 1996 the search was carried out by the police. From July 1996 to February 1998 various investigative steps were taken, also relating to five co-accused in the case, for example searches in Denmark, Switzerland and Sweden.

In the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases’ (selskabstømmersager) came into existence in Denmark. It covered a criminal activity by which the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud. The persons involved were usually intricately interconnected and collaborated in their economic criminal activities, which concerned very large amounts of money. According to surveys made by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Danish kroner (DKK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. Following a number of legislative amendments, the trade in inactive, solvent companies largely ceased in the summer of 1993.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32848/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The Court declared the application admissible by a decision of 9 October 2007. At the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases” (selskabstømmersager) came into existence in Denmark. It covered a criminal activity by which the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud by buying up and selling numerous inactive solvent private limited companies within a short period. Police carried out an investigation between 1994, 1995 and 1996. The applicant was charged on forty-four counts out of a total of fifty-nine, committed between 26 June and 3 November 1992. The indictment related to eighty different companies and six banks in Denmark and abroad. More than seventy witnesses were heard, including state-registered public accountants. Statements of accounts and a considerable amount of other documentary evidence were also produced. The court records comprised 1,330 pages. The closing speeches were held over ten days in November. The case was set down for trial on 15 March 1999. A total of 119 hearings were held. The trial lasted between 15 March and 31 January 2001. The applicant was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. The sum of DKK 3,600,000 was seized, and he was deprived for an indefinite period of the right to establish a private limited company. The City Court dismissed the applicant’s claim that the length of the proceedings had been at variance with Article 6 of the Convention. The complexity of the acts carried out by [the applicant and the five co-accused] partly when buying and “stripping” the companies for assets, partly when writing off projects abroad, necessitated an investigation of an extraordinary scope. In the City Court's opinion there were no longer periods, whether before the police or the prosecution, during which no part of the case proceeded. The trial commenced on 24 September 2002. Most of the hearings took place in 2003 and 2004. A total of about 90 hearings were held in the case. The Court records comprised 861 pages. The High Court upheld the City Court’s judgment. The applicant and the co‑defendants requested that the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) grant them leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) Three of the defendants stated in their petitions that they would submit supplementary comments, which were received on 17 December 2004. The cases were sent to the prosecution, which gave its opinion on 29 March 2005. Nothing happened in the case until 2 May 2006, when the police telephoned the Leave to Appeal Board and drew attention to the case. The applicant and the co-defendant were informed on 21 June 2006 that their requests for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court had been refused. At the same time, the board apologised for the length of the proceedings before it. to an error, nothing happened for more than a month before they were referred back to the police. The application was settled in July 2006, and the case was settled out of court in January 2007. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who was found guilty of unlawful possession of a weapon and sentenced to 18 months imprisonment.

It follows from the definition that this is manifest in the patient's personality from the time he or she becomes an adult. The person in question perceives the disorder as part of his or her own self, the motivation for change is usually insufficient. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994, and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. The applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. Finally, he is to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the countymedical officer. The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The order took effect immediately, but the applicant failed to report to the hospital; the police accordingly took him there on 16 March 1995. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. According to the record of a hearing held in camera on 20 April 1999, the applicant explained that before 1994 he had had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. During his period at large, he had taken precautions against spreading the disease. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. He lost all sexual desire and would in future have to decline all sexual relations. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. He used to go shopping once a day, usually for beer, and [the witness] would estimate that he had drunk between four and six cans of beer every day. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. The applicant had been in contact with a chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., who was not connected to the hospital. After the applicant's involuntary return, P.N. had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant had made a lunge at him. A statement of 8 April 1999 by B.S., a psychologist at the special care facility at the hospital who had met the applicant once, found that the applicant was intellectually above average. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years.” “In conclusion, in the county medical officer's opinion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease,” the court found. “During [the applicant's] contact with the doctors in question, they did not discuss the risk of spreading the disease at all” The applicant appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated: “The opinions [by other psychiatrists and one psychologist] resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [the applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol.” On 12 June 1999 the applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. The application was made after a large explosion at a checkpoint in County Derry. Five British soldiers and one civilian were killed and a number of other British army personnel were seriously injured. It was suspected that the bombing had been carried out by the Irish Republican Army (an unlawful paramilitary organisation known as the IRA) The applicants were, in turn, suspected by the police of membership of that organisation and of involvement in the bombing. Both applicants were cautioned by police officers in the usual terms, namely that they were not required to say anything unless they wished to do so. They were also informed that anything they did say would be taken down in writing and might be given in evidence against them.

The applicants were suspected of involvement in the bombing of a British Army checkpoint in County Derry in October 1990. The applicants were cautioned that anything they did say would be taken down in writing and might be given in evidence against them. The High Court ruled that the applicants were not required to say anything unless they wished to do so. They were acquitted of all charges against them on October 25, 1990. However, the applicants still face charges of conspiracy to commit an act of terrorism against the British government. The application was dismissed on October 27, 1990, and the case was heard again on October 30, 1990 and October 28, 1990 respectively. The appeal was heard by the Supreme Court and dismissed.

A large explosion occurred at a British Army/Royal Ulster Constabulary checkpoint in County Derry on 23 October 1990. Five British soldiers and one civilian were killed and a number of other British army personnel were seriously injured. Irish police officers on surveillance duty noted a light in a house approximately four miles from the scene of the explosion. At approximately 6.05 a.m. on 24 October 1990 a warrant was obtained to search the house. The seven men in the house, including the owner and the applicants, were arrested and detained by the police under section 30 of the Offences against the State Act 1939 (‘the 1939 Act’) As later noted by the High Court, it was suspected that the bombing had been carried out by the Irish Republican Army.

applicants were brought to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin and charged with the offence of membership of an unlawful organisation. Each was convicted of failing to provide an account of their movements during a specified period contrary to section 52 of the 1939 Act. Both applicants were sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The applicants then appealed against their conviction and sentence under section 52 to the Court of Criminal Appeal. They argued that section 52 should have been read as including the possibility of a refusal to give information based on reasonable excuse. The High Court rejected their application. It based the applicants' right not to answer questions as regards their movements on Article 38 of the Constitution rather than on Article 40.

Each of the applicants brought an action in the Labour Court, claiming outstanding salaries, dismissal indemnities, severance pays and other pecunities. Court ordered municipality to pay the following amounts in Turkish lira (TRL), including costs, together with interest running from June 1999: i. TRL 915,737,870 to Abbas Baran; ii. TLR 880,824,998 to Mehmet Bayram Ceylan0; i. TLL 1,062,932,278 to M. Cihat Aydın; iv. TRR 911,348,350 to M, Ali Ağın, v. TLRs 1,111,150,000 to Mustafa Yağmur; vi. TLT 935,170,454 to Hasan Buğa; vii. TLM 833,474,812 to Fuat Albayrak; viii. TLRM 1,078,451,254 to Ahmet Hüseyinoğlu; ix.TLR 1,021,383,958 to Enver Askan; x. TLr 905,829,494 to Hamdusela Ekinci. No settlement was reached with the other applicants. However, the municipality deposited certain partial amounts in the relevant account at the local enforcement office. Amounts were made available to some applicants and later paid to others. On 9 November 2004 a settlement agreement was reached by the applicants' representative, Mr Sedat Çınar, and the authorities. Cihat Aydın initiated fresh claims against the municipality to recover their severance pay.

His parents were lawfully employed and have meanwhile acquired Austrian nationality. The applicant attended school in Austria. In late 1998 criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. He was, inter alia, suspected of having broken into cars, shops and vending machines, of having stolen empties from a stock ground, and of having forced another boy to steal 1,000 Austrian schillings from the latter’s mother. On 7 September 1999 the Vienna Juvenile Court (Jugendgerichtshof) convicted the applicant of some 22 counts of partially completed and partially attempted aggravated gang burglary.

He stressed that he had come to Austria at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and was not able to speak Bulgarian. He had no relatives and other social contacts in Bulgaria and drew attention to the fact that he was still a minor. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the residence prohibition was justified under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 22 December 2003 the applicant was deported to Sofia.

eval_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first and third applicants were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 (“the 2000 Act”) on suspicion of involvement in the murder of a police officer on 9 March 2009. They were detained at Antrim police station on the same day. On 16 March 2009 the Director of Public Prosecutions made applications to the County Court under paragraph 29 of Schedule 8 to the 2000 Act for warrants of further detention in respect of both applicants. Court Judge granted warrants authorising a five-day extension of detention. In her reasoning, Judge Philpott noted that the relevant forensic evidence was central to the investigation and that the investigation was being carried out diligently and expeditiously. The second applicant was arrested under section 41 of the 2000 Act on suspicion of involvement in the murder of two soldiers at Masserene Barracks, Antrim, on 7 March 2009. He was detained at Antrim Police Station on the same day. Following a hearing on 16 March 2009 a County Court judge granted a warrant extending the second applicant’s detention as the results of a number of forensic tests were pending. On 21 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court for a seven-day extension to the period specified in the warrant for further detention. Neither the interviews nor the results of the forensic tests provided any evidence linking the second applicant to the murders of the two soldiers. The applicants sought permission to apply for judicial review of Judge Philpott’s decisions of 21 and 22 March 2009 granting further extensions to the warrants authorising their detention. The High Court of Northern Ireland heard the applications on 25 March 2009. The review of the lawfulness of the detention had to embrace an examination of the basis of the arrest, otherwise a person could be detained under the 2000 Act for up to twenty-eight days without there having been any judicial review. High Court of Northern Ireland quashed decision to grant extensions. Admitted review of lawfulness of arrest need not involve analysis of basis for arrest. Court held that the ‘competent legal authority’ referred to in Article 5 was the magistrate in the United Kingdom. The court found that, although there was no express power to order release in the 2000 Act as required by Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, such a power must be implied. There was no provision for conditional release on bail within the statutory scheme, an issue which did not arise in the present case but would need to be addressed in any future case. The High Court of Northern Ireland ruled that there was no authority which supported the applicants’ contention that Article 5 required that a detained person be charged well before the expiry of the twenty‑eight day period contemplated in the 2000 Act. The court found that there were a range of tools available to the court to preserve to the necessary extent an adversarial procedure and equality of arms. The ruling was made on 24 February 2011 and the case was heard for the first time on 4 April 2011. It was the first hearing of the case in the UK since it was heard in 2010. The judge said it was a case of ‘general public importance’. The applicants were released without charge on 25 March 2009. The first and third applicants were not subsequently charged with any offence related to the murder of the police officer. The second applicant was immediately rearrested and interviewed over the following two days. On 27 March 2009 he was charged with the murder. of the two soldiers, five attempted murders and. possession of a firearm and ammunition. His application for bail was refused. The High Court refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. On 7 November 2011 the second applicant stood trial before a judge sitting without a jury. On 20 January 2012 he was acquitted on all counts of the indictment.

Four armed robbers stole 120,000 French francs (FRF) from a transport company. An employee gave information to the robbers in return for FRF 10,000. A judge issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for less than eight days. In a judgment of 27 November 1996 the Indictment Division of the Versailles Court of Appeal indicted the applicant and committed him for trial at the Assize Court. That order was served on the applicant on 3 October 1996. The judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release and made a partial discharge order.

Four armed robbers wearing masks entered the premises of a transport company. They forced the company manager, whom they had taken hostage, to open the safe. They stole 120,000 French francs (FRF) in cash before making off. The investigators concentrated their inquiries on some of the prison inmates. One of them, G.D., had witnessed the offences and been threatened by the robbers. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn-off shotgun.

The judge issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for less than eight days. In a judgment of 27 November 1996 the Indictment Division of the Versailles Court of Appeal indicted the applicant and committed him for trial.

The applicant requested that a bailiff be called on to record officially that his detention had become unlawful. The last order extending it, effective from midnight on 19 September 1996 for a period of four months, had expired on 19 January 1997. The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on grounds of appeal based, firstly, on an infringement of Article 725 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, secondly, on a breach of Articles 201 and 214 of the code of criminal Procedure and Article 5 of the Convention. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the Indictment Division had not ruled on the facts being investigated and that the warrant of commitment issued by the investigating judge continued to have effect.

The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on grounds of appeal based, firstly, on an infringement of Article 725 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, secondly, on a breach of Articles 201 and 214 of the code. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on 19 January 1995 a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of the applicant’s case”

The applicant was detained by the Indictment Division for four months after the Versailles Court of Appeal’s judgment of 27 November 1996. He appealed on points of law, relying on grounds of appeal based, firstly, on an infringement of Article 725 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, secondly, on a breach of Article 5 of the Convention. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on 19 January 1995 a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of the applicant. …” In the same judgment the Ind indictment Division ordered that the applicant should be kept in custody to avoid all risk of pressure being brought to bear on witnesses or collusion.

In 1996 the investigating judge extended the detention of the applicant three times for four months, the final extension taking effect on 19 September 1996. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. On 10 September 1997, after completion of the further investigations, the Indictment Division directed that the applicant be committed for trial at the Yvelines Assize Court charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. The case continues. The applicant was arrested in January 1995 and charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence. A forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, along with a sawn-off shotgun. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn off shotgun. In January 1997 the applicant requested that a bailiff be called on to record officially that his detention had become unlawful. On 9 April 1997 the applicant made an application to the Indictment Division for his immediate release on the ground that he was being detained arbitrarily. Four Turkish nationals, Mr Atalay Dede, Mr Mehmet Kumral, Mr Hüseyin Hakkı Zabcı and Mehmet Akın Dirik complained about the length of the proceedings against them. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) In 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) . This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section.

The case originated in an application (no. 32981/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the proceedings against them. By a decision of 17 October 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The case was heard by a three-judge panel with the judge elected in respect of Turkey sitting as an ad hoc judge. The Government and the applicants each filed observations on the merits.

The case originated in an application (no. 32981/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 17 October 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled that the application was admissible on the basis of the merits of the application. The case was settled in favour of the applicants.

The applicants were accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol. The Ankara Martial Law Court convicted the applicants and sentenced them to terms of imprisonment. The applicants appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) It quashed the convictions of Mr Dede and Mr Dirik and referred the cases to the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court. The cases are referred to the Turkish Criminal Code under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish criminal code. The applications are still awaiting trial.

The applicants were accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The Ankara Martial Law Court convicted the applicants and sentenced them to terms of imprisonment. The applicants appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court. I. The circumstances of the applicants' arrest and detention in 1981. The conditions of their detention on remand. The charges against the applicants. The proceedings on appeal. The cases on appeal and the verdicts. The convictions of Mr Mehmet Kumral and Mr Hüseyin Hakkı Zabcı. The conviction of Mr Dede and Mr Dirik.

The applicants were accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) On different dates the applicants were all released pending trial by the Ankara Martial Law Court. The applicants appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) The cases are still pending before the latter court. The applications have been referred to the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) for further proceedings. The cases have been sent to the Court ofCassation after martial Law was abolished in 1994. The decisions of the Cassation have not been made public.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32981/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the proceedings against them. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The Court declared the application admissible in October 2000. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The Government of Turkey was represented by their Agent, Ambassador Tugay Uluçevik. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled that the application was admissible. The Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) was accused of being an illegal organisation. The applicants were accused of membership of an organisation whose aim was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. They were all released pending trial by the Ankara Martial Law Court. On 19 July 1989 the applicants were convicted and sentenced to terms of imprisonment. The cases are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi) The applicants appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) and the cases were sent to it. It quashed the convictions of Mr Dede and Mr Dirik and referred the cases.

The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Izmir. He was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of involvement in various acts of arson with a view to protesting against the arrest of Abdullah Öcalan. The applicant, who was not represented by a lawyer, repeated his earlier statements and gave details about each set of events. He also accepted the contents of his police statement and verbatim records of a reconstruction of events that had been carried out. He admitted that after each act they had called the television station MED TV to claim responsibility under the name of “Apo’s tigers of revenge”.

The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Izmir. On 18 March 1999 the applicant was arrested and taken into police custody. In the verbatim records, signed by the applicant, the latter admitted, inter alia, to taking part in three separate acts of arson together with Mr M.K. and Mr F.D. In order to protest against the arrest of Abdullah Öcalan, the former leader of the PKK (Workers’ Party of Kurdistan), an illegal armed organisation. After each act they had called the television station MED TV to claim responsibility under the name of ‘Apo’s tigers of revenge’

The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Izmir. He was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of involvement in various acts of arson with a view to protesting against the arrest of Abdullah Öcalan. The applicant was questioned by two police officers in the absence of a lawyer. In the verbatim records, signed by the applicant, the latter admitted, inter alia, to taking part in three separate acts of. arson together with Mr M.K. and Mr F.D. They were accused of setting fire to a car on 19 February 1999 and two buildings on 13 and 14 March 1999. The first-instance court held its first hearing, in the presence of the applicant and his lawyer, on 11 May 1999.

On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judges sitting on the bench of the State Security Courts were replaced by civilian judges. At the second hearing held on 19 August 1999 the judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time. On 17 August 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment as regards the applicant’s conviction for arson. It, however, quashed the conviction as regards his conviction under Article 169 of the Criminal Code on the ground that, in view of the statements of the accused, partially accepted before the pre‑trial stage, he had made admissions which incriminated him.

The applicant retracted his earlier submissions, claiming that he had made them under duress. He also contested the verbatim records of the reconstruction of events and other evidence which incriminated him. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment as regards the applicant’s conviction for arson. It, however, quashed the conviction on the ground that, in view of the statements of the accused, partially accepted before the pre‑trial stage, it was partially accepted. The applicant and his lawyer submitted that they repeated their earlier submissions. On the same day, following the parties’ statement that they did not wish any additional investigation to be carried out, the prosecutor submitted his observations on the merits.

The applicant was convicted under Article 168 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to 12 years and six months' imprisonment. The applicant appealed. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. By letter dated 16 June 2008 the applicant’s representative informed the Court that the applicant was no longer in prison. The application was dismissed and the applicant is currently serving his sentence in a prison in the city of Bursa, Turkey. The case was referred to the Izmir State Security Court on 9 November 2000. The applicant was convicted under Article 168 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to 12 years and six months' imprisonment. In his petition, he submitted that, apart from evidence obtained under duress at the pre-trial stage, there was no evidence to demonstrate that he had taken part in these acts. He further complained that there was nothing to indicate that he was part of an illegal organisation and that therefore Article 168 should not have been applied to him. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicant’s representative informed the Court that the applicant was no longer in prison on 16 June 2008.

James Malone was charged with offences relating to dishonest handling of stolen goods. His trial, which took place in June and August 1978, resulted in his being acquitted on certain counts and the jury disagreeing on the rest. He was retried on the remaining charges between April and May 1979. Following a further failure by the jury to agree, he was once more formally arraigned; the prosecution offered no evidence and he was acquitted. On 28 February 1979, the Vice-Chancellor, Sir Robert Megarry, dismissed the applicant’s claim (Malone v. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (No. 2), [1979] 2 All England Law Reports 620; also reported at [ 1979] 2 Weekly Law Reports 700).

name: Philippe Bidart
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52363/11) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the restriction on freedom of expression imposed on him in the framework of his release on licence was contrary to Article 10. The application was communicated to the Government on 5 September 2013. The case was decided on 9 October 2013 and the ruling was published on 9 November 2013. It was decided that Mr Bidart was not entitled to a hearing because he had been granted a licence to speak in public. The decision was made in favour of the applicant and he was awarded the right to appeal.

The application was communicated to the Government on 5 September 2013. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr François Alabrune, Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court of Appeal will hear the case from the end of January 2014.

The applicant is the former head of the Basque separatist organisation Iparretarrak. He was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in the framework of terrorist activity, killing two members of the State security police force (“CRS”) In 2007 the Sentence enforcement division of the Paris Court of Appeal released him on licence from 14 February 2007 to 14 February 2014, ordering to follow a seven-year programme of assistance and supervision. The Government pointed out that the applicant was the first person sentenced toLife imprisonment for offences linked to terrorism ever to have been released on licence. The applicant’s release on licence would be accompanied by the following general obligations: complying with the instructions of the sentence enforcement judge or of the social worker from the Prison rehabilitation and probation service.

Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention, which forms an integral part of the domestic law, specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court’ This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

Gerhard W. Luedicke was convicted of a road traffic offence in 1972. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. He applied to the European Court of Human Rights to have the charges against him dropped. The court found that the charges were not proven and that he should not have to pay them. The U.S. Embassy in Berlin is seeking to have his case thrown out of the Court of European Human Rights. The British Embassy in Germany is seeking a temporary restraining order to get the case overturned. The case is being heard by the European Commission of Human rights in Strasbourg, France, on May 22 and 23, 2013.

Some courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that while the Code of Criminal Procedure exempts an accused from paying in advance, it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

The applicant, represented by the Command Legal Aid Section at Bielefeld, entered an appeal (Erinnerung) against this assessment of costs. The appeal was dismissed on 31 August 1972. The object of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention ... is to guarantee certain fundamental rights to everyone faced with criminal proceedings. Under German procedural law, however, no accused person need make advance payment for the costs of interpreters. This would appear not to be the case in this case. Under the rules of German criminal procedure every person finally convicted must himself bear all the costs, including ... the interpretation expenses. This obligation is not contrary to Article 6.

The paintings in issue show an orgy of unnatural sexual practices (sodomy, bestiality, petting), which is crudely depicted in large format. They are liable grossly to offend the sense of sexual propriety of persons of ordinary sensitivity. The artistic licence relied on by the appellant cannot in any way alter that conclusion in the instant case. The content and scope of constitutional freedoms are determined on the basis of the federal law currently in force. This applies inter alia to freedom of the press, freedom of opinion and artistic freedom. The Cantonal Court scrutinised the paintings for a predominantly aesthetic element. It decided that the emphasis was on sexuality in its offensive forms. The Cassation Division of the Federal Court agrees. The overall impression created by Müller’s paintings is such as to be morally offensive to a person of normal sensitivity. The appeal against the confiscation order was inadmissible as it had not first been made before the cantonal courts. The appellants maintained that the publication element of the offences was lacking. They are wrong. The obscene paintings were on display in an exhibition open to the public which had been advertised on posters and in the press. There was no condition of admission to ‘Fri-Art 81’, such as an age-limit. Swiss law says confiscation is a preventive measure in rem. Court: A more lenient order may thus be justified where it achieves the desired aim. Confiscation remains however the rule. It should be departed from only where a morelenient order achieves the needed aim. “almost eight years later’, the court said. The court preferred a ‘more lenient measure which achieved the aim of security, whilst complying with the principle of proportionality’. The Federal Court held that a measure should not remain in force where the circumstances justifying it cease to obtain. The decision was based on the Basle-Urban Court of Appeal of 19 August 1980. Josef Felix Müller recovered his paintings in March 1988. The confiscation measure was not absolute but merely of indeterminate duration, which left room to apply for a reconsideration. It appears to the court that the preventive measure has now fulfilled its function, namely to ensure that such paintings are not exhibited in public again without any precautions. Once the order has achieved its aim, there is no reason why it should continue in force. Accordingly, the artist is entitled to have his works returned to him. It is not necessary to attach any obligations to this decision. If J.F. Müller decided to exhibit the three paintings again elsewhere, he knows that he would be running the risk of further action by the courts.

The applicant was represented by Ms C. Almond, a lawyer practising in Dublin. The Irish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr P. White, of the Department of Foreign Affairs. On 4 January 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was written to the Irish Human Rights Commission, which was granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party.

The applicant was born in 1978 and has a permanent address in Dublin. The criminal proceedings against the applicant to which this application relates arose, inter alia, from his association with the following events. An off-duty Garda (police) detective attached to the Special Detective Unit - who lived in a housing estate near Dublin called Corke Abbey - noticed suspicious activity and contacted a local Garda station. He watched the movements of three cars (a blue Nissan Almera, a dark Nissan Micra and a yellow Transit van) and he noticed the occupants of the three cars acting in what appeared to be a coordinated manner. An unmarked Garda vehicle manned by two Gardaí arrived in response to the off- duty detective’s call and approached the van. While speaking with the driver of the Transit van, they noted a black balaclava and the handset of a portable radio. The other Garda opened the back door of the van and saw the other four men, sitting on the floor, as well as a number of items (which the trial court later regarded as “ significant pieces of evidence’.

Five men of the original eight who remained in the estate, and who were in the Ford Transit van, were arrested and charged with being members of an illegal organisation. The Nissan Micra car which had left Corke Abbey after dropping off three of the five men who had been in it, was later traced back to a Ms K., the partner of the applicant (see paragraph 22 below).
