The applicant was brought before the Special Criminal Court (“SCC”) and charged with membership on 10 October 2002 of an unlawful organisation, the IRA. He and a co-accused (NB) were interviewed at length by police officers. The trial court later noted that the two accused accepted that they had had full access to legal advice and found that each had availed himself of the opportunity to consult a solicitor before and during several police interviews. On 18 November 2004 the SCC delivered its judgment convicting the applicant and his co- accused. The SCC said that there were four strands of evidence tendered by the prosecution: (i) the sworn testimony of Chief Superintendent PK that it was his belief that the applicant was a member of the IRA; (ii) evidence that associated each of the accused with the activities at Corke Abbey which the prosecution contended were of a type usually associated with the IRA and which it claimed supported or corroborated PK’s evidence; and (iv) inferences, it argued, that could properly be drawn.

The applicant was brought before the Special Criminal Court (“SCC”) and charged with membership on 10 October 2002 of an unlawful organisation, the IRA. He and a co-accused (NB) were interviewed at length by police officers. Numerous questions were put to them concerning the events in Corke Abbey and the evidence gathered by the police. The trial court later noted that the two accused accepted that they had had full access to legal advice and found that each had availed himself of the opportunity to consult a solicitor before and during several police interviews. On 18 November 2004 the SCC delivered its judgment convicting the applicant and his co- Accused.

The SCC ruled that the applicant was guilty of being a member of the IRA contrary to section 21 of the 1939 Act.

PK claimed privilege stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security. The SCC directed the Chief Superintendent to produce all relevant documentation which, he asserted, informed him that the accused were members of the IRA. The Court conducted a review of those files considering this to be the most appropriate solution in the interests of justice. It found that there was nothing in the files that would assist the defence in proving the innocence of their clients. Later, in weighing PK’s evidence, the SCC was satisfied that PK had “adequate and reliable information” on which he could legitimately form the opinion that each accused was a member of the Provisional IRA.

The applicant made an application for an inquiry into PK’s sources arguing that his trial would be unfair if he did not know these sources and the evidence against him. When asked to identify his sources, he claimed privilege stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security. The SCC directed the Chief Superintendent to produce all relevant documentation which, he asserted, informed him that the accused were members of the IRA. In compliance with the direction, files relating to both the applicant and his co-accused were produced to the trial court, but not disclosed to the prosecution or to the defence. The Court conducted a review of those files considering this to be the most appropriate solution in the interests of justice.

The prosecution, which had no access to the confidential source material, opposed the applicant's request on the basis of the principle of informer privilege. Chief Superintendent PK was the person best placed to learn of the activities of the accused. He had 25 years’ service as a police officer most of which was devoted to combating subversion. SCC confirmed that it had excluded any information to which it had become privy during its review of the files he had produced to the court. The SCC was persuaded beyond any doubt by the belief evidence of PK that the accused were members of the IRA as charged. It was difficult to imagine anyone better informed on the subject in the country. The trial court was satisfied that PK had formed that belief ever before the ‘Corke Abbey’ events of 10 October 2002 or any matters discovered following the arrest.

The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. It was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. The trial court accepted that the documentation established that the applicant was, at the very least, acquainted with the driver of the Transit van (PB) and the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) However, it was not, of itself, supportive of Chief Superintendent PK’s evidence that the applications was a member of the IRA. A thumb print on black tape found in the almera was accepted as being that of the co-accused.

The trial court had no doubt that the applicant was either one of the male drivers of the Nissan Micra at Corke Abbey or that he was aware of and acquiesced in the use to which it was being put. It was also satisfied, having heard abundant evidence which included sightings of the applicant and his co-accused together in the middle of the night when the applicant’s home was being searched, that they were ‘well known’ to each other. Each man failed to answer a variety of questions which, the court maintained, were very material to the investigation of the offences with which each was charged. The video-recordings of the interviews were shown to the trial court. It noted that, not only did each remain totally silent during the course of interview, but each appeared to take no ostensible interest whatsoever in what was going on. They sat bolt upright showing remarkable self-control throughout, in that their only movement was an occasional blink of the eyes but they made no effort to engage with the interviewers. The court was satisfied that not only were the relevant statutory provisions invoked and adequately explained to each accused but each was given an opportunity to protest in the event that he had not understood that explanation.

Chief Superintendent PK was entitled to claim privilege in respect of underlying facts or sources which led to his belief that disclosure of same could cause a credible threat to life or to state security. The exercise of the trial court’s discretion to review the files furnished by the Chief Superintendent PK did not infringe the right to a fair trial. It found no evidence that would have assisted the accused and the material examined constituted a good basis for the belief of the Chief superintendent. The belief of PK was simply admitted as being evidence, no more and no less, and this was already well established in the prior jurisprudence. The trial court had confirmed that, if it had found otherwise, this would have led to a different outcome.

The facts upon which the trial court relied were all proven beyond reasonable doubt. The CCA considered that their objection, against a background of a total failure to answer any question at all, was rather surreal. The trial court was fully entitled to have found that the applicant was associated with the events at Corke Abbey and its conclusion, in the circumstances, was a safe and valid one. He requested the court to certify that its previous decision involved a point of law of exceptional public importance and that an appeal should be taken to the Supreme Court. The CCA reviewed the case law of this Court upon which the applicant had relied. It concluded that the approach taken by the Court was in the public interest. The applicant brought an application to the CCA under section 29 of the 1924 Act, pursuant to which he requested the court to certify that its previous decision involved a point of law of exceptional public importance. The question proposed by the applicant for the Supreme Court’s consideration was whether the receipt and examination of material concerning the applicant to which neither he nor his advisors had access was consistent with the State's obligation to provide a fair trial. The CCA reviewed the case law of this Court upon which the applicant had relied and refused the application for a section 29 certificate. It concluded that the approach taken by the Court was in the public interest.

applicant brought an application to the CCA under section 29 of the 1924 Act. He requested the court to certify that its previous decision involved a point of law of exceptional public importance. The CCA reviewed the case law of this Court upon which the applicant had relied. It found that the entitlement to disclosure is not an absolute right and that, in any criminal proceedings, there may be competing interests, such as national security or the need to protect witnesses at risk of reprisal. It concluded that the approach taken by this Court was the correct one and that the trial judge held a supervisory role in determining the balance between the competing rights of the defence and of public interest immunity.

The CCA rejected the submission that the trial court’s approach involved a review of material which was determinative of guilt. Rather, the judges were considering whether PK's evidence should be admitted without cross-examination as to its source in circumstances where privilege was invoked. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence. If the SCC had found documents of assistance to the applicant, its answer would have been different, the CCA said. The undisclosed documents were demonstrably not determinative as the applicant had suggested. The trial court had explicitly stated this to be so in its judgment.

CCA: The exercise of the trial court’s discretion to review the files furnished by the Chief Superintendent PK did not infringe the right to a fair trial. It found no evidence that would have assisted the accused. The material examined constituted a good basis for the belief of the Chief. Superintendent. The CCA rejected the submission that the SCC, which decided on guilt or innocence, should not have carried out this review having regard to this Court's case-law. It was not at The CCA held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. A statement to the contrary was explicitly made by the court and was to be found in judgment itself. The court was fully entitled to have found that the applicant was associated with the events at Corke Abbey and its conclusion, in the circumstances, was a safe and valid one. The evidence established a complete and utter failure to answer any question at all and the court’s entitlement to draw inferences arose, precisely, from that failure. The commentary as to demeanour did not alter that in any way. The court found that the evidence was sufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that both men were members of the IRA. But it ruled that the right to silence did not apply. The case was taken to the Supreme Court, which ruled that it was not in the public interest to reveal the full extent of the links between the IRA and the suspects. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the defendants and the case was remanded back to the trial court for further action to be heard. The Supreme Court ruled the evidence had been proven and that the case should be re-examined. The decision was handed down on November 20, 2007. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court. In weighing up the value of that belief evidence, the trial judges had had no regard at all to the documentary source material. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence and it was clear from the SCC's review that there were no such documents. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38713/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the conventions. The President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 7 February 2007. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3, it was decided to examine the merits of the Application at the same time as its admissibility. The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) was passed in 1989. The ECHR is the only body that can grant benefits to people outside the European Union. The ECHR was established to protect the right of the European Parliament to vote on issues relating to human rights and human rights. The European Parliament has a right to a voice in the decision making process, including the right to an appeal if a decision is not in line with the ECHR’s founding principles. The right to appeal is also a fundamental right, and can only be won if the case can be shown that the decision is fair and just. In the case of the EHR, the case was that of the right not to give a benefit to a person.

The law provides that only adults with children can claim benefits. The law has been amended to allow fathers to claim benefits for their children. The current law does not provide for the right to claim such benefits for children under the age of five. It also does not allow the right of parents to claim the benefits for the sake of their children, even if the child is under five years old. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that the law is not legally binding, and that it should be amended to make sure it is legally binding. The World Economic Forum has said that the current law is unconstitutionally vague and therefore does not apply to children of any age.

The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) was signed into law in 1989. It was meant to protect the right of EU citizens to a fair trial. But the ECHR has since been amended to remove the right to a trial by jury. The European Court of Human Rights has now ruled that the law does not apply to EU citizens. The ECHR is now considering whether the law should be amended again to include a provision for a child’s right to sue the government if it is found to be “inadequate” or “unduly restrictive’ of the rights of the child. The ECHR has already held that the “right to sue’ is not a right, but a “privilege.

The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31) Antun Petrovic claimed a parental leave allowance (Karenzurlaubsgeld) in 1989. He argued that section 26(1) of the Unemployment Benefit Act 1977 provided that only mothers could claim such an allowance when a child was born. The Court heard addresses by Mr Marxer, Mr Laimer and Mr Okresek. The Commission produced various documents from the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 October 1997. The circumstances of the case were laid out below. The Constitutional Court held that section 26(1) did not infringe the applicant’s constitutional rights and was not contrary to Article 8 or Article 12 of the Convention. It added that even if regard was had to recent statutory amendments (section 26 of the Unemployment Benefit Act had been amended by a federal law of 12 December 1989 – see paragraph 15 below), the applicant's complaint was unfounded. The legislature had a certain amount of time in which to adapt new rules to changes in society (Anpassung gesetzlicher Vorschriften an geänderte Verhältnisse), the court said.

The applicant claimed that both sets of repairs constituted trespass to his property. He claimed he was entitled to damages in the sum of GBP 100,000. The council brought proceedings in the Sheriff Court (the civil court of general jurisdiction). The applicant filed a counter-claim alleging that the council had instructed further repairs that had damaged his property, and sought referral of the case to the Court of Session.

A fire damaged the applicant's flat and part of the flat below belonging to a commercial property company. The applicant refused to pay the council for his share of the repair costs. The council brought proceedings in the Sheriff Court (the civil court of general jurisdiction) and the applicant filed a counter-claim alleging that the council had instructed further repairs that had damaged his property. On 14 November 1994 the sheriff court upheld the council’s claim, rejected the applicant’S counter- claim and found that the case did not meet the criterion for referral to the Court of Session. In 1998, the applicant brought proceedings against the architect and chief executive of the preservation company for contempt of court in relation to an alleged failure to produce documents in the initial action. By judgments of 17 February 1999, the Sheriff court rejected the applicants claims.

The first and second defenders were served on 14 May 1997. Defences were lodged by both defenders on 12 June 1997. The parties’ written pleadings were open and closed at the request of the parties. The applicant was then informed by the court that, since part of his claim challenged one of the orders made in the Sheriff Court proceedings, he was required to intimate a copy of the closed record to the relevant sheriff clerk. On 26 February 1998, the court gave him leave to do so. There was then further correspondence between the parties as to the future procedure in the case, which led the applicant to apply to the court for an order for disclosure of certain documents.

The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. By a decision of 14 May 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment at Norwich Crown Court in 1989. The two men were charged with conspiracy to commit murder. The pair claimed that they were not involved in the crime, but had been paid to carry it out. The case was settled out of court and the pair were acquitted of all charges against them. They were sentenced to three years in prison, but were released after serving one year. The other two men are still awaiting trial for their part in the alleged crime. The jury could not reach a verdict because of a lack of evidence. The trial was adjourned until April 2008 and the men were released on bail. They are still fighting for the right to keep the money they were paid for. Government says evidence in the Nugent case fell into two categories. The first type of evidence derived from the Holmes computer system used by the police officers conducting the murder inquiry to store and cross-reference all the information obtained in the course of the inquiry. The second category of evidence related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent. The Government submitted that, following the applicant’s conviction, and in the light of developments in the common-law duty of disclosure (see below), the prosecution reviewed their position and decided that the data stored on the computer system did amount to disclosable material. Document no. 580 subsequently came into the applicant’s possession. No reason was given to explain the decision to include the document in the list of withheld evidence. Counsel for the defence was in contact with the prosecution concerning possible further disclosure. The prison psychotherapist’s report of 31 January 2000 noted that the applicant had been referred in December 1999 given her distress and difficulties in coping with her imprisonment. It noted as follows: “Largely confined to a wheelchair, [the applicant] manifests obvious physical symptoms of cerebral palsy as well as somewhat less obvious mental ones.” “She often strikes those who meet her as an individual with a normal range of mental functioning but a difficult personality,” it added. “From the view point of those who deal with her, it often may seem that she is being difficult or uncooperative when it is in reality the case that she simply has not fully grasped the nuances of the subject at hand” The applicant was detained in the medical wing of the prison since the normal prison cells were not wheelchair accessible. Behrens and Ms K. Behr. After the match had ended the police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams. The applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. The public prosecutor reopened the investigation and ordered further enquiries. A further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including fourteen platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. Germany, which was the applicant’s name. The crimes were committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 and in Göttingen on 3 February 2007 respectively. The applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, robbed its occupants. He was sentenced to a total of nine years and six months in prison, and imposed an accumulated prison sentence (Gesamtfreiheitsstrafe) of 9 years and 6 months. The court found it established that in the evening of 14 October2006 the applicant entered by force into a Kassel apartment and robbed the occupants. The men were aware that the apartment was used for prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. O. and P. were friends of L., one of the victims of the crime committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006, and they had both worked for some time as prostitutes in the Kassel apartment rented by L. before moving to Göttingen. The two men reported to the residual members of the criminal gang that they had spotted a safe in the apartment’s kitchen. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. B. left the apartment at around 8.30 p.m. taking the money. Regional Court notes that the records of O. and P.’s interrogations at the investigative stage showed that they had given detailed and coherent descriptions of the circumstances of the crime. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The court further emphasised that when taking into account the testimonies given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friend L. it had paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence and had to be assessed particularly carefully. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. However, their own statements at trial had at least confirmed that one of them had visited the apartment at Göttingen on the evening before the crime. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he followed P. when she escaped over the balcony and explained that he had done so in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems. (“Totalausfall des Fragerechts”), they had as a whole been fair and there had been no reason to exclude the witness statements as evidence. The Regional Court had assessed the contents of the records of the witnesses’ testimonies read out at trial particularly carefully and critically. In view of the various layers of corroborating evidence the applicant had had ample opportunities to put into question the credibility of the two main witnesses and to effectively defend himself. Uli Lutz, born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49 of the Regulations. Mr. Lutz was given a fine (Geldbusse) of DM 125.

Mr. Lutz had himself admitted to the police that he was not expecting the car which was moving out to the left onto the road in front of him to make a U-turn. He had consequently attempted to overtake it but had been unable to avoid a collision despite his efforts to brake. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury. The applicant was convicted of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) and sentenced to nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The court based its findings on DNA expert evidence pointing to a high probability that the applicant had been the person that had caused marks found at the crime scenes and on further circumstantial evidence.

The applicant was arrested on suspicion of committing robberies in February 2000. He was detained pending trial, which began on 19 October 2000. At the end of the fifth day of the trial, the court set the next trial hearing for 17 November 2000 at 9 a.m. The court, following a proposal made by the applicant’s counsel, promised a penalty of less than ten years’ imprisonment in exchange for the applicant's waiver of claims over confiscated assets. The Court convicted the applicant of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) and sentenced him to nine-and-a-half years' imprisonment.

After delivery of the judgment, the court verbally informed the applicant of his right to lodge an appeal on points of law. In the applicant’s presence, counsel for both the defence and the prosecution waived their rights to appeal. As the applicant had not been aware of the invalidity of his waiver, he could not be held responsible for having failed to comply with the statutory time-limit of one week for lodging an appeal. The Court of Justice did not find it necessary to establish whether the waiver had been part of a negotiated agreement, as this fact did not call into question the validity of the waiver as such. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Refugee Board (Flygtningenævnet), which on 16 April 1999 requested the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to provide more information on the situation in Iran. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 13 September 1991 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 13071/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 29 September 1986. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 June 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Clarke and Mr Campbell for the applicant. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. The jury’s decision was by a majority verdict of ten to two. He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. Leave to appeal against the sentence but not the conviction was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 5 February 1985. On 21 May 1985 the substantive appeal against sentence was dismissed by the full court. In February 1986, the Director of Public Prosecutions decided that there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges against the police officers. At the disciplinary hearing, on 13 to 15 June 1988, the tribunal decided there was no case to answer and dismissed the case. An independent police investigation into the case was ordered in the course of which certain facts came to the attention of the court. The report was requested by the Home Department but its disclosure was refused on the grounds of public interest. Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) referred the applicant’s case to the Court of Appeal under section 17 (1)(a) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968. The reference was heard on 18 July 1986 and judgment delivered on the same date. 21 March 1986, the Secretary of State for the Home Department referred the applications to the Appeal Court. The applicant was convicted of burglary but found not guilty by reason of miscarriage of justice. The appeal court found that the verdict should be set aside because of certain shortcomings in the prosecution case, in particular, that certain information had been withheld by the police. In fact two fingerprints had been found which later turned out to be those of the next door neighbour who was a regular visitor to the house. The Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. It was of the opinion that, even if these matters had been investigated, it would have made no difference to the outcome. The court concluded as follows: “It is clear that there was some slipshod police work in the present case, no doubt because they took the view that here was a man who had admitted these crimes fully, and consequently there was very little need for them to indulge in a further verification of whether what he said was true.’” “We do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions.”

The applicants behaved aggressively, loudly expressing opinions about the purpose and nature of the intervention. As the applicants were interfering with the arrest of D. S., they were hit with truncheons. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He had insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. Police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. All the facts had been established on the basis of the arguments of police, who had apparently been instructed by police lawyers as to what they should say. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor concluded that the contested decision had to be upheld.

eval_texts: Mary and Alan Wainwright applied to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. They complained that they had been strip-searched when seeking to visit a relative in prison, relying on Articles 3 and 8. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The Government made comments on just satisfaction of the applicants' claims. By a decision of 13 December 2005, the Chamber declared the application admissible. Governor ordered all Mr O’Neill’s visitors be strip-searched before visits. The applicants were taken across the courtyard from the south gatehouse by four or five prison officers. One of the officers stated that they had reason to believe that the applicants were carrying contraband. The first applicant was told to take off her jumper and vest. She was then instructed to remove her shoes, socks and trousers, which she did. The second applicant was beginning to be distressed and the first applicant tried to calm him down. They were then taken to separate rooms for the searches. Although there were roller blinds on the windows, they were not pulled down. The first applicant was crying. She was standing naked apart from her underwear. She believed that anyone outside the prison looking at the windows in the room where she was being strip-searched could have seen her in a state of undress. Although none of the officers touched her, she felt threatened by their actions. She considered that she had no alternative but to comply with their instructions. The first applicant told the officers that she might as well sign it as there was by that stage nothing else the officers could do to her. She then did so without reading it. The search of the second applicant was taken to a separate room by two male officers. The applicants were led back to the prison to proceed with their visit. During the visit, the first applicant told Mr O’Neill what had happened. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The second applicant felt shaken and nervous and was upset. On returning home, she removed her clothes and bathed because she felt upset, angry and dirty. Because of her experience, she did not visit Mr O'Neill for a further four months. In October 1998, in the context of the civil proceedings, she was examined by Dr Sims, Professor of Psychiatry. Dr Sims considered that the severe upset that she had experienced in the prison made her existing depression (for which she was receiving medication at the time of the visit) worse. The first applicant was suffering from post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depressive illness. The second applicant was also suffering from PTSD. Both illnesses had been substantially caused by his strip-search experience. The County Court upheld the applicants’ civil claims against the Home Office, holding that the searches constituted a trespass to the person which the person had been searched for. The case continues at: http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/features/article-261538/Home-Office-strips-two-prisoners.html#storylink=cpy. This article has been amended to make clear that Dr Sims concluded that the first applicant had PTSD and that the second applicant had depressive symptoms. We are happy to clarify this. Court of Appeal allowed Home Office's appeal on 20 December 2001. First applicant awarded 2,600 pounds sterling (GBP) and the second applicant a total of GBP 4,500 (comprising GBP 3,500 basic damages and GBP 1,000 aggravated damages), the Home Office having conceded battery following the trial judge’s factual findings. Lord Chief Justice Woolf noted that there were numerous ways in which drugs could be smuggled into prison and that the most vigorous regime of searching prisoners would not in itself suffice. He found therefore that a search of Mr O’Neill would have been inadequate. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances. House of Lords upheld the judgment of the Court of Appeal and dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The court set aside the first-instance judgment and substituted an award of a total of GBP 3,750 to the second applicant for battery. Lord Hoffmann, delivering the leading judgment, found that there was no infringement of Article 3 as the conduct had not been sufficiently humiliating to constitute degrading treatment. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which the prison officers were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. Lord Hoffmann writes that there is no evidence that the adoption of some high level principle of privacy is necessary to comply with Article 8 of the Convention. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case in which it considers that there has been an invasion of privacy contrary to Article 8. The court expressed some impatience, at paragraph 103, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of privacy invasion. But in my opinion it shows no more than the need, in English law, for a system of control of the use of film from CCTV cameras which shows greater sensitivity to the feelings of those caught by the lens. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. Sections 6 and 7 of the Act are in themselves substantial gap fillers. If it is indeed the case that a person’s rights under Article 8 have been infringed by a public authority, he will have a statutory remedy. This is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle. For these reasons I would reject the invitation to declare that since at the latest 1950 there has been a previously unknown tort of invade of privacy.

The case was heard at the National Court of Justice in Szczecin, Poland, on 20 October 2005. The trial was adjourned until 25 January 2006. The judge ruled that the applicant could be released on bond. The application was settled at the Court of Appeal of the Republic of Poland, where the applicant was granted bail. The appeal was dismissed on 15 July 2004.

The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Szczecin. He was arrested on suspicion of having committed several offences of drug trafficking. In the course of the investigation, his detention was extended several times. In their decisions the courts referred to the complexity of the case and the fact that many suspects were involved and some of them had not yet been arrested. They stressed that the detention was justified by the need to analyse the existing evidence and the scope of the applicant’s criminal activity. However, at the same time it ruled that the applicant could be released on bail on payment of a security. The applicant appealed against the decision extending his detention but to no avail.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13378/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that, when the first of them died, the survivor would be required to pay inheritance tax on the dead sister’s share of the family home. The survivor of a married couple or a homosexual relationship registered under the Civil Partnership Act 2004 would be exempt from paying inheritance tax in these circumstances. The application was allocated to a Chamber within the Fourth Section of the Court. On 12 December 2006 the Chamber unanimously declared the application admissible and delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation.

The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8, 10 and 13. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Istvan Herczegfalvy is a Hungarian citizen who has lived in Austria since 1964. He currently resides in Vienna. He served two prison sentences in succession, following convictions pronounced by the Vienna Regional Criminal Court (Landesgericht für Strafsachen) and confirmed in part by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) He was declared partly incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser by the Inner Vienna District Court (Bezirksgericht Wien Innere Stadt) on 23 December 1975. The Court heard addresses by them on 21 April 1992. Mr Herczegfalvy was detained after he had finished serving his sentence in 1977. A psychiatrist’s report had been drawn up following numerous complaints by him about prison conditions. The applicant unsuccessfully appealed to the Review Chamber (Ratskammer) of the Regional Court and to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), whose rulings were given on 18 May and 21 June respectively. According to a ruling of the guardianship court of 19 July 1984, his position was equivalent as from 1 July 1984 to that of a curator (Sachwalter) within the meaning of Article 273 (3), sub-paragraph 3, of the Civil Code. The hearing before the Regional Court took place on 9 and 10 January 1979. The court found that the charges against Mr Herczegfalvy had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 45 below) The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia querulans which from 1975 at least had been equivalent to a mental illness. The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained, but in prison, on the psychiatrist’s recommendation. On 10 September 1979 he was admitted to ward 23 of that hospital, and stayed there until his release on 28 November 1984. On 4 December 1979 Mr Herczegfalvy requested his release. On 14 December the investigating judge informed him that he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. He said that he had made them only with a view to his repatriation to Hungary, which was discussed on 6 November 1980 but did not take place. In 1980 he withdrew his appeal and application for a declaration of nullity in writing on 30 October 1980. The judgment was on the latter date declared binding by a final order. On 8 February 1982 the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr Herczegfalvy’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. On 16 February 1984 the latter court ordered a further extension of the detention in issue. Taking into account the opinions of the psychiatric expert and the director of the hospital, filed on 25 January 1984, it considered that there had been no fundamental change in the applicant's mental state. He was still suffering from paranoia querulans, and if released would undoubtedly refuse to follow the necessary course of treatment. Mr Herczegfalvy had begun a hunger strike on 2 August 1979 as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed on 28 August and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On 10 September 1979 he was transferred back to the Vienna psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release on 28 November 1984 (see paragraph 23 above). He was injected by force with 90mg of Taractan on 15 January 1980, in order to bring about a state of somnolence (Dämmerschlaf) in which it would be possible to treat him by means of perfusions. Mr Herczegfalvy. made a complete recovery when he left, and he still needed treatment with antibiotics and neuroleptics. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making. The restraints were not removed until 14 February 1980. On 22 February he was given paper and a ballpoint pen. On 27 December 1980 he was forbidden to watch television. On 12 November 1982 he stated that he no longer needed to be fed artificially, as a doctor had persuaded him to end his hunger strike by explaining to him that it was endangering his life. An expert noted the progress which the applicant had made and expressed the opinion that troublesome behaviour did not constitute a risk within the meaning of Article 21 of the Criminal Code. The director of the hospital advised the court not to terminate Mr Herczegfalvy’s detention as the treatment carried out, based on medication, had only a sedative effect. The Regional Court thereupon on 16 February 1984 refused to release the applicant. He eventually recovered his liberty on 28 November 1984, after a further expert report dated 14 September 1984 (see paragraph 23 above).C. The control of correspondence while in detention and the restrictions on access to information. The measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law. They had been justified for therapeutic reasons, and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion. The measures had been taken for disciplinary purposes only, the Government said. They were not intended to be permanent and only lasted a short period of time. They have now been removed from use in all but one of the hospitals they were used in. The other two hospitals have not been affected by the measures. These were the Bournemouth Royal Infirmary and Northampton General Hospital. The hospital has been the subject of a review into the measures taken in both cases.

The Polish Government (the Government) were represented by their Agents, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki and, subsequently, by Mr Jakub Wołąsiewicz. The applicant was detained on remand until 21 January 1995. The Gdańsk Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 31 March 1995. An expert opinion on the state of the applicant's mental health was issued on 21 November 1994. The court found that in view of the seriousness of the offence he was charged with, the strong probability of his guilt and the danger that he (or another member of his group) would exert additional pressure on the witnesses, the applicant was warranted. On 5 April 1995, the judge ruled that the applicant should be released on bail. On 12 April 1995 the court ordered the applicant to undergo psychiatric observation. The judge also ruled that this should be extended until 30 June 1995. The bill of indictment was lodged with the Gdańsk Regional Court against the applicant and eleven co-accused. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. The court remarked that the negative effect of the continuing detention upon his family situation was not such as to call for his release. In a separate set of criminal proceedings, the applicant was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine. He served his sentence between 15 March 1996 and 11 September 1997. The hearing was adjourned in view of the absence of the applicant’s lawyer. The case was heard in the Gdańsk Regional Court from 9 November 1995 until 22 November 1996. The regional court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention until 30 June 1997. The Supreme Court granted the Regional Court's request on 16 January 1997. On 13 August 1997 the Supreme court, relying on the grounds given above, prolonged the applicant's detention. However, the limit of the duration of the detention was set at 1 December 1997 and not at 31 December 1997 as the Regional court had requested. The hearing scheduled for 25 September 1997 was adjourned as one of the hearing dates had been cancelled due to the illness of the accused. The case was complex and multi-layered and the charges of a serious nature. Some of the accused had contributed to the overall length of the proceedings by lodging motions with the court. In these circumstances, even though the proceedings in the case had been lengthy, the Regional Court could not be held responsible for this delay. On 22 October 2002 the court gave a judgment by which the applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71932/12) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation would subject him to inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to expel the applicant to Hungary until further notice. On the same day the Court. decided to communicate the application to the Austrian Government and to grant priority to the application under. Rule 41 of the rules of Court. It further requested the Hungarian Government to provide information regarding the status of the applicant’s asylum. proceedings, as well as the reception conditions for unaccompanied minor asylum-seekers in Hungary. The applicant claims he was forced to lodge an asylum request and placed in an open camp in Hungary. Allegedly, the Hungarian authorities did not give any consideration to the fact that he was a minor. He left the camp two or three days later and took a train to Vienna. He claimed not to know the status of his asylum proceedings there because he was illiterate. The Traiskirchen Federal Asylum Office (Bundes­asylamt – hereinafter “the Asylum Office’) rejected the applicant’s asylum request. On 11 January 2012 the Asylum Court (Asylgerichtshof) quashed that decision pursuant to Article 66 of the Code of General Administrative Procedure. On 28 February 2012 the Asylum Office rejected the applicant’s asylum request and ordered his expulsion to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation. Hungary expelled asylum-seekers to Serbia, if their first asylum proceedings were terminated and there was no obstacle under the non-refoulement rule. If a detained refugee claimed to be a minor, an age assessment was ordered and the minor was released if his or her age was confirmed. Hungary did not practise refoulement to Serbia. The Hungarian authorities had assumed jurisdiction. over the applicant's asylum request under Article 16. § 1 (c) of the Dublin. II Regulation, which proved that the applicant still had access to asylum. proceedings on the merits in Hungary. Hungary's asylum proceedings in Hungary had been discontinued on 24 October 2011. The first asylum proceedings would not be reopened upon his return to Hungary. If he was returned to Hungary, an asylum request would be considered a subsequent request which would not have automatic suspensive effect if there were no new circumstances supporting his application but there was a safe third country which he could be returned to. At that time, the applicant was still a minor. An arrest order stated that a transfer of the applicant to the Hungarian authorities was planned for 22 November 2012. On 20 November 2012 the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court and requested the Austrian Government to stay the applicant’s transfer to Hungary until further notice. The applicant was placed in a children’s home in Fót, where care and education were provided to them according to their age. The Court notes that on 1 January 2014 Regulation (EU) No 604/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council (“the Dublin III Regulation”) entered into force. At the time of the decision by the Austrian authorities to expel the applicant to Hungary, the Dublin II Regulation was the applicable legal basis. The aim is to avoid multiple applications and to guarantee that each asylum-seeker's case is dealt with by a single member State. The applicant would turn 18 on January 2013, it was very unlikely that a guardian would be appointed for him upon his return. The member State responsible for examining an asylum application of an unaccompanied minor shall be that where a member of his or her family is legally present, provided that this is in the best interests of the minor. The asylum application must be rejected as inadmissible if, under treaty provisions or pursuant to the Dublin Regulation, another State has jurisdiction to examine it. International documents describing the conditions of detention and reception of asylum-seekers in Hungary are extensively summarised in the judgment in Mohammed v Austria (no. 2283/12, §§ 32-50, 6 June 2013) The UNHCR was also particularly concerned about Hungary and concluded that it maintained its previously expressed concerns regarding Hungary’s ongoing practice of treating asylum claims as second applications. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee commented on legislative changes in Hungary which entered into force on 1 July 2013. It raised concerns that there might be a threat that asylum-seekers were placed in alien policing detention upon return to Hungary. Asylum-seekers who applied for asylum immediately upon their arrival, or at the latest during their first interview with the immigration police, were no longer detained. Those who failed to apply immediately, or who otherwise failed to communicate such an intention, continued to be subject to detention for the duration of the entire asylum proceedings. In addition, access to asylum proceedings in Hungary had improved for those asylum‑seekers transferred to Hungary under the Dublin system whose claims had not been examined and decided. Hungarian Helsinki Committee noted that following the changes in legislation in January 2013 Dublin returnees were now considered as first-time applicants. They had the chance to substantiate the reasons for their application in a detailed ‘in-merit procedure’ and were not detained. Those asylum-seekers who had withdrawn their application, or had received a negative decision on the merits, may however be placed in immigration detention after being returned under the Dublin II Regulation. From 1 July 2013, pursuant to Act XCIII of 2013, the Asylum Act provides for a newly created detention regime called ‘asylum detention’. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee concluded that the amendments introducing a separate detention regime for Asylum-seekers seriously weakened the judicial review of immigration and asylum detention and the right to appeal in asylum proceedings. The maximum period of asylum detention is six months. Vulnerable people were not excluded from detention, with the exception of unaccompanied children. Alternatives to detention were available in the form of bail, a designated place to stay, and periodic reporting obligations. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee criticised that the scope of application of bail as alternative to asylum detention was not defined clearly enough, which it feared could result in the non-application of this measure in practice. It examined some of the detention orders and observed that the Office of Immigration and Nationality failed to carry out a proper individual assessment of the cases before subjecting asylum-seekers to detention. It criticised that detention orders did not contain any justification why alternatives to Detention were not used, despite such alternatives being obligatory under the law. Detainees complained about inadequate housing conditions, lack of equipment and cleaning materials, inadequate water quality and difficulties in practising their religion. There were complaints of a lack of access to specialist medical care. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention expressed its concern that there had been a significant focus on detaining asylum-seekers. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee noted that following the changes in legislation which took effect in January 2013, deportation could no longer be imposed on Asylum-seekers during the asylum procedure. It noted that the Government had responded in the last few years with different approaches to the influx of people crossing Hungary’s borders. Unaccompanied minors remained exempted from detention. The issue of prolonging the detention of an asylum-seeker and the lack of proper judicial review were consistently raised during interviews it conducted. The right to a complaint which could be submitted against a detention order was not often explicitly communicated to those being detained. Detention should not be the common and first resort and should be for the shortest possible duration, especially when genuine asylum-seekers may be overlooked or detained unnecessarily without proper justification. It recommended that the measures introduced by the recent law, which were considered to be positive, should be implemented in a clear and defined manner. The Working Group called to the Hungarian Government’s attention the fact that the situation needed robust improvements and attention to ensure against arbitrary deprivation of liberty.

The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The application was dismissed on appeal on 25 May 2009. The Government was represented by their Agent, Ms J. Gladstone, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. He was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment”. The applicant also provided answers to all the questions which he had declined to answer during the police interviews in March and June 1997. The judge directed the jury as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to proveAnything” The judge concluded with the following direction: “I have to tell you as a matter of law, that the fact that a defendant tells a lie, is not of itself, evidence of guilt.” The judge went on to deal with the questioning of the applicant by the police. In this regard, he noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying “no comment” to each of the questions posed. The applicant did not suggest that he was advised by his lawyer not to comment but said that he did not want to incriminate people in relation to stolen vehicles. He admits that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing, inter alia, that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) On 18 June 1998 the jury found the applicant guilty of the offences charged. He was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adetoro was involved in the sixth robbery and ignored his assertion he was with Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson at the time of the robbery. The application was dismissed on the grounds of insufficient evidence and the applicant was acquitted of all charges. The appeal was dismissed again on the basis that there was insufficient evidence. The Court of Appeal handed down its judgment on 21 June 1999. It agreed that there had been no need for a Lucas direction. However, it considered that the fact that one was given did not prejudice the applicant's defence or the safety of his conviction. On 20 July 2005, the Criminal Cases Review Commission (“CCRC”) referred the applicant’s conviction to the Court of appeal on the basis of the trial judge's direction to the jury. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the applicant had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. Jury must also have rejected the applicant's explanation of why he failed to answer questions in the police interview, says the court. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary direction which, in the event, provided assistance to the jury in how to approach the question. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The judgment of the Court of Appeal found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming. The judge concluded: “This was not therefore a case in which one could say that the correct direction would have tipped the balance”. The case was settled out of court in a settlement worth around £1.5 million. The applicants are a same-sex couple living in Vienna. They requested the Office for Matters of Personal Status (Standesamt) to proceed with the formalities to enable them to contract marriage. The Vienna Municipal Office (Magistrat) refused the applicants’ request. The applicants lodged an appeal with the Vienna Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann), but to no avail. In his decision of 11 April 2003, the Governor confirmed the Municipal Office’s legal view. On 12 December 2003 the Constitutional Court ruled in favor of the applicants. The case was decided in the High Court of Justice (HJ), Vienna.

A same-sex couple living in Vienna were denied the right to marry. The applicants argued that marriage had evolved since the entry into force of the Civil Code in 1812. Other European countries either allowed homosexual marriage or had otherwise amended their legislation in order to give equal status to same- sex partnerships. They argued that in the event that one partner in a homosexual couple died, the other was discriminated against since he would be in a much less favourable position under tax law than the surviving partner in married couple. The case was decided by the Constitutional Court on 12 December 2003 and the decision was published online on 17 April 2004. The legal impossibility for them to marry constituted a violation of their right to respect for private and family life and of the principle of non-discrimination.

In addition, the following thirteen member States do not grant same–sex couples access to marriage. The European Parliament and the Council of 29 April 2004 concerns the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the member States. The legal consequences of registered partnerships vary from being almost equivalent to marriage to giving relatively limited rights. The possibilities for registered partners to undergo medically assisted insemination or to foster or adopt children vary greatly from one country to another. In two States, namely Ireland and Liechtenstein, reforms intending to give same-sex couples access to some form of registered partnership are pending or planned. Croatia has a law which recognises cohabiting same- sex couples for limited purposes, but does not offer them the possibility of registration. Slovenia, Switzerland and the United Kingdom also offer the possibility to register a registered partnership. In most of the States concerned, registered partners obtain a status similar to marriage. This also applies to other material consequences.

On 25 September 2000 the Assize Court upheld the decision that there was no case to answer.

The applicant was born in 1953 and lives in Wiśniowa, Poland. The applicant’s father lodged an application with the Myślenice District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) for distribution of the inheritance from his late wife in 1989. Between October 1989 and December 1992 the court held four hearings. The Kraków Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal in 2000. The Supreme Court refused to deal with her cassation appeal in 2001. The case was settled out of court in 2000, and the applicant was awarded the amount of her father's inheritance, but the amount is not yet known.

train_texts: The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that the European Union can take action against any country that fails to comply with the EU’s “right to freedom of expression’. The European Court has ruled the right of the EU to take action to “prosecute’ any breach of the European Convention on Human Rights. The EU can also take legal action against countries that fail to adhere to the European Charter of Fundamental Rights, which includes the right to free speech, freedom of association and freedom of the press. The World Court ruled in 2008 that the EU can’t take action without the permission of the countries’ governments, and can only do so if they have agreed to abide by the rules. This is the case with the European Commission.

The International Commission on Human Rights (ICHR) was set up in 2004 to deal with human rights abuses. The International Commission is based in Geneva, Switzerland, but it has expanded to include many countries. The international commission is also based in Germany, the UK, France, the U.S. and Canada. It is responsible for international human rights law, including the right to a fair trial, and the freedom of speech. The ICHR was established to promote human rights in the world, and to provide a forum for human rights activists to air their views. It was also set up by the International Commission to protect human rights, including human rights to freedom of expression, privacy, and freedom of movement.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20089/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor’s fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time and that the Regional Appeals Commission which dealt with his case was not impartial and independent. The claims against the Lower Austrian Health Insurance Board amounted to 8,022.41 euros (EUR) and EUR 6,603.81, respectively. The application was dismissed on 25 February 1999 and the applicant appealed against that decision. The President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 7 May 2008. An amendment to the Social Insurance Act (Allgemeines Sozialversicherungsgesetz) entered into force on 1 September 2002. It provided for changes in the composition of the Regional Appeals Commission. On 17 May 1999 the applicant filed an application for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag), requesting a decision on his submission of 5 October 1998. On 27 November 2000 the Constitutional Court set aside the decision for violation of the right to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. It noted that one of the assessors had negotiated the clause on remuneration for laboratory tests on behalf of the Lower Austrian Medical Association. . The decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. The mere fact that the assessors were members of Regional Medial Associations or Regional Health Insurance Boards did not suffice to cast doubt on the independence and impartiality of the Regional Appeals Commission. The fact that one member of the Commission had been involved in the negotiation of the general agreements, gave rise to legitimate doubts about that member’s independence. Such special circumstances had not been shown by the applicant in the present case. The case was heard at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, on 13 November 2005, and the decision was delivered on 2 December 2005.

Mr Smolney said he had been instructed by a man called Mr Morgan to bring the black suitcase, which he believed to contain antiques, from Sao Paolo to Heathrow and to leave it on the luggage carousel. In pursuance of Article 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Canton of Vaud (CPP/VD), all investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The reason for the confidentiality of judicial investigations is the need to protect the interests of the criminal proceedings by anticipating risks of collusion and the danger of evidence being tampered with or destroyed. The present case concerns secrecy imposed by the law rather than by an official decision. However, disclosure to friends or relatives by the parties or their lawyer is not punishable (see Article 185a CPP/VD).

The cantonal court found that while the accident of 8 July 2003, the circumstances of which were undoubtedly unusual, had triggered a great deal of public emotion, it had nevertheless, in legal terms, been simply a road accident with fatal consequences. The court concluded that the appellant had the professional duty (under former Article 32 of the Criminal Code) as a journalist to publish the information.

It was not a case of collective trauma on the part of the Lausanne population, which would have justified reassuring the citizens and keeping them informed of the progress of the investigation. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest in the disclosure of classified information. This type of information provides no relevant insights into the accident or the circumstances surrounding it. It relates to the private life, or indeed intimate sphere, of the person in custody, and it is difficult to see any interest which its publication could satisfy other than a certain kind of voyeurism. The same applies to the appellant’s requests to the investigating judge in relation to his choice of defence lawyer.

It was not a case of collective trauma on the part of the Lausanne population, which would have justified reassuring the citizens and keeping them informed of the progress of the investigation. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest in the disclosure of classified information. The letters virtually exclusively concerned criticisms levelled by the accused against his lawyer and such practical problems as requests for temporary release, for access to personal effects, to change cells and to use the telephone. This type of information provides no relevant insights into the accident or the circumstances surrounding it. It is difficult to see any interest which its publication could satisfy other than a certain kind of voyeurism.

It is true that the ‘Lausanne Bridge case’ attracted extensive media coverage. However, this circumstance alone, alongside the unusual nature of the accident, is insufficient to substantiate a major public interest in publishing the confidential information in question. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest. This finding of fact, which the appellant has not disputed in his public-law appeal, is binding on this court (see section 277 bis of the Federal Criminal Procedure Act). That being the case, the appellant fails to demonstrate the 'obvious’ interest to the general public of the information published.

The court ruled that the tone adopted by the appellant in his article showed that his main concern was not, as he claims, to inform the general public about the State’s conduct of the criminal investigation. The headline of the article (‘Questioning of the mad driver’, ‘the reckless driver's version’) already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author's view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a ‘mad driver”. The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the fact that the journalist was trying to make himself impossible to defend.

Article 293 of the Criminal Code punishes only the disclosure of information, irrespective of how the perpetrator obtained it. The other two factors relied upon by the appellant concern his behaviour (good faith in access to information and mode of publication) The European Court of Human Rights reiterates that neither it, nor the domestic courts for that matter, should substitute their own views for those of the press as to what technique of reporting should be adopted. In weighing up the interests at stake it nevertheless takes account of the content, vocabulary and format of the publication, and of the headings and sub-headings (whether chosen by the journalist or the editors), and the accuracy of the information.

The article suggested that the case had already been tried in the author’s view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a ‘mad driver’, a man ‘oblivious to the events and all the hubbub around him’.
